content.title: How To Invest In SpaceX Before Its IPO —And Why Your Structure Matters
content.text: TOPSHOT - SpaceX Starship lifts off from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, for its sixth flight test on November 19, 2024. SpaceX aborted an attempt to catch the first stage booster of its Starship megarocket in the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower, opting instead for an ocean splashdown, a live feed showed November 19. The hitch came as President-elect Donald Trump joined SpaceX chief Elon Musk at the company's Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas to watch the test flight, the latest sign of the budding bromance between the two billionaires. (Photo by CHANDAN KHANNA / AFP) (Photo by CHANDAN KHANNA/AFP via Getty Images)AFP via Getty ImagesSearches for how to invest in SpaceX, how to buy SpaceX stock and SpaceX IPO have accelerated sharply in 2026 for a simple reason. There is still no publicly traded SpaceX common stock, but the possibility of an IPO now looks more concrete than at any prior point. Reports indicate that SpaceX is preparing for a potential listing as early as June 2026, with sources discussing a valuation approaching $1.75 trillion — potentially 40% higher than the company's most recent reported pricing. Plans could still change.The investment thesis expanded further in February 2026 when SpaceX acquired xAI in a deal valuing SpaceX at $1 trillion and xAI at $250 billion, creating a combined entity worth about $1.25 trillion. For investors, that broadened the narrative from launch systems and Starlink satellite internet to a platform spanning space infrastructure, connectivity and artificial intelligence.So when investors ask how to buy SpaceX stock, the technically accurate answer remains: Direct public ownership is not yet available. Investors can evaluate the main structures through which SpaceX exposure is currently accessible and assess which of those structures is best positioned to capture returns when a listing occurs.For investors searching how to invest in SpaceX before an IPO, the key question is no longer whether exposure exists, but which structure offers the most effective way to access it.Access to SpaceX is no longer the primary challenge. The universe of available vehicles has expanded dramatically, and investors can now access SpaceX-related exposure through an EFT, closed-end funds trading on the NYSE, a closed-end interval fund, a traditional open-end mutual fund or through direct secondary market platforms. But each of these structures reflects profoundly different trade-offs across cost, liquidity, lock-up risk and the investor’s ability to act when prices are strongest. In private markets, how an investment is structured can be as consequential as the investment itself.Why Investors Can’t Buy SpaceX Stock YetInvestors are not yet able to buy SpaceX stock directly through a normal brokerage account. SpaceX remains a private company. Retail investors cannot purchase SpaceX common stock the way they buy shares of Apple, Nvidia or Tesla. That is why high-intent searches for how to invest in SpaceX are really searches for the closest practical substitute: a fund, vehicle or structure that offers some form of exposure before a public listing.The central question is not simply which vehicles provide SpaceX exposure. It is which structures allow an investor to act when that exposure may be most valuable. Historical IPO data suggests that, on average, the most attractive exit window has tended to occur during the first few months after a listing, before lock-up periods expire. Investors who are structurally locked in during that window cannot benefit from it, regardless of their analytical conviction — though, SpaceX-specific factors may alter that pattern.Why The Lock-Up Window Matters MostBefore evaluating any SpaceX investment vehicle, investors should ask one question first: Does this structure allow me to act after an IPO, or does it lock me in during the period when prices have historically been strongest? That single question is worth answering before evaluating any other variable. It is the organizing framework of the analysis that follows — though SpaceX presents factors that may complicate the usual answer. With that filter in mind, the available options fall into a clear hierarchy for retail investors. Listed funds with daily liquidity and no post-IPO lock-up come first. Funds with quarterly redemption windows come next. Closed-end funds trading at large net asset value premiums introduce a separate and additional risk. Secondary market platforms — which impose the most direct lock-up constraints — are restricted to accredited investors and are addressed last.There are four broad paths investors typically consider, ranked here by retail accessibility and lock-up risk:1. ETFs and mutual funds with daily liquidity: Available to any retail investor through a standard brokerage account. No post-IPO lock-up. Investors can buy and sell freely, including during the pricing window immediately following a SpaceX IPO. This is the most structurally favorable category for investors who prioritize the ability to act. While the ETF and Mutual Fund structures offer certain advantages related to liquidity and pricing, with ETFs having a few liquidity and tax advantages compared to mutual funds, they may not be appropriate for all investors, particularly those seeking concentrated or direct private market exposure.2. Closed-end funds listed on public exchanges: Retail-accessible, with daily trading and no post-IPO lock-up. However, these funds frequently trade at large premiums to their underlying net asset value — a distinct and material risk that is entirely absent from ETFs. Investors buying at an extreme premium are betting on that premium sustaining, not simply on the underlying portfolio.3. Interval funds: Retail-accessible, priced at NAV with no premium risk, but redemptions are limited to periodic windows that may be subject to quarterly caps — commonly up to 5% of assets, though terms vary by fund. If SpaceX peaks in the months immediately following its IPO, redemption windows may not align with the moment an investor would want to act.4. Secondary market platforms (accredited investors only): Provide the most direct SpaceX exposure, but are not available to general retail investors and impose post-IPO lock-up periods of six to twelve months — the precise window when historical data shows prices have been strongest and then declined. These are covered last in this article, as they are inaccessible to most readers.Why Lock-Ups Can Shape Investor OutcomesThe case for prioritizing liquidity over direct access begins with the data. Large-capitalization technology IPOs have followed a remarkably consistent pattern across more than a decade: prices surge in the early months following a listing, often reaching their peak within three to six months, then decline materially as lock-up restrictions expire and early investors are permitted to sell.The critical detail is timing. The peak pricing window — when gains have historically been greatest — falls during the exact period when investors who entered through secondary platforms, SPVs, or other locked structures are contractually prohibited from selling. By the time those lock-ups expire and those investors can act, the most favorable window has typically already closed. The table below documents this pattern across 15 major U.S. technology IPOs.US Large Cap Tech IPO's—Pre and Post Lockup PerformanceEntrepreneurShares LLCThe averages are striking. Across 13 completed observations, these stocks rose an average of approximately 132% from their IPO price to peak levels, yet investors holding through lock-up expiration captured only approximately 26% from the original IPO price — after enduring a drawdown of approximately 44% from those peaks. In most cases, the historically strongest pricing window had already passed before locked-up investors were permitted to act.The Structural ImplicationAn investor who could act during the peak pricing window and an investor locked into holding through lock-up expiry faced dramatically different outcomes — not because of different analytical skill, but because of different investment structures. For a company like SpaceX, where demand at IPO is expected to be exceptional and expectations are already elevated, this dynamic is likely to be amplified.It is important to note, however, that historical IPO patterns do not determine SpaceX’s outcome. Some companies continue to surge well past the lock-up expiration date, and investors who sold early may have left substantial gains on the table. Facebook — later rebranded as Meta — is the clearest example: investors who exited during or shortly after the lock-up period would have missed one of the most sustained growth cycles in the history of large-capitalization technology. Over the decade following its 2012 IPO, Meta grew from a post-IPO price of approximately $38 to over $500, a compound return (over 13x) that dwarfs whatever was captured by those who sold into early-cycle strength. The historical averages in the table above reflect central tendencies, not guarantees. A company with SpaceX’s scale, market position, and narrative could follow either trajectory.There is a second, SpaceX-specific factor worth considering: S&P 500 index inclusion. Under a fast-track exception available to companies meeting certain profitability criteria, SpaceX could potentially qualify for inclusion in the S&P 500 at some point after its IPO. The scale of that possibility is notable. Estimates suggest that between index funds, ETFs, and institutional mandates benchmarked to the S&P 500, somewhere in the range of $15 to $20 trillion in assets currently tracks the index. If SpaceX were to enter the index at a valuation of $1.5 trillion or more — implying a weighting broadly comparable to Tesla’s — the implied index weight could approach 2%, potentially generating $300 to $400 billion in demand from index-tracking mandates alone against an expected tradeable float of perhaps $50 to $75 billion. That is a level of structural demand with few historical precedents. However, S&P 500 inclusion itself requires meeting float and liquidity thresholds that may not be satisfied until well after the IPO — potentially coinciding with or following the expiration of the lock-up period, as locked-up shares enter the market and the tradeable float expands. In that scenario, the index inclusion demand and the lock-up expiry supply could arrive together, with uncertain net effect. The interaction between these forces — IPO demand, lock-up expiry, and index inclusion timing — makes it genuinely difficult to predict when, if ever, SpaceX stock might reach its peak after going public.The table below ranks many popular SpaceX investment vehicles by a criterion the IPO data above identifies as potentially consequential: whether the investor retains the ability to act after a listing. Retail-accessible structures with no lock-up appear first. Structures with quarterly redemption windows follow. Secondary market platforms — which impose the longest lock-up periods and are restricted to accredited investors — appear last.SpaceX Pre IPO OptionsEntrepreneurShares LLCEFTs Offer Daily Liquidity And No Lock-UpFor retail investors, the ETF structure is the most accessible starting point: no minimum investment requirement, no post-IPO lock-up, no accreditation requirement, and daily intraday liquidity through any standard brokerage account. ETFs, open-end mutual funds, and listed closed-end funds all provide daily exit flexibility — the key distinction is that ETFs and open-end mutual funds carry no lock-up constraints, while closed-end funds introduce NAV premium risk as a separate variable.XOVR — The ERShares Private-Public Crossover ETFXOVR carries a strong conviction position in SpaceX, estimated at approximately $205 million. The fund’s public portfolio is drawn from the ER30TR Entrepreneurs Index, a rules-based benchmark of founder-led public companies. Investors require no accreditation and can invest through standard brokerage and retirement accounts. As with all investments, investors should review the current prospectus before investing.Mutual Funds Provide Daily Liquidity And Broader DiversificationOpen-end mutual funds are a second retail-accessible category offering daily liquidity and no post-IPO lock-up constraints. They require no accreditation and are available through standard brokerage and retirement accounts. SpaceX exposure within these funds varies by manager and portfolio construction, and investors should review current holdings disclosures for each fund. For investors whose objective is broad portfolio diversification that also includes SpaceX exposure, this structure may be appropriate.Baron Partners Fund (BPTRX)Baron Partners Fund (BPTRX) holds SpaceX as part of a diversified portfolio, with daily liquidity, a $2,000 minimum investment, and approximately 1.3% in annual expenses. No post-IPO lock-up applies.Morgan Stanley Counterpoint Global Insight Fund (CPOAX)The Morgan Stanley Counterpoint Global Insight Fund (CPOAX) holds SpaceX alongside a broader portfolio of public and private companies, with a $1,000 minimum investment and approximately 1.4% in annual expenses. Daily liquidity is provided under normal conditions with no post-IPO lock-up.Closed-End Funds Trade Daily But Carry Premium Risk Closed-end funds with SpaceX exposure trade daily on public exchanges and require no accreditation. Investors should be aware that these funds have, at times, traded at large premiums to their underlying net asset value (NAV), though the size of that premium has varied considerably.Why a NAV Premium Is a Distinct RiskClosed-end fund premiums are historically mean-reverting. When a premium contracts, investors may experience a loss even if the underlying portfolio appreciated over the same period. The loss comes not from what the fund owns, but from what investors paid to own it. Investors should understand this distinction before purchasing shares at a premium to NAV.Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ)Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a closed-end fund holding a portfolio of private technology companies, with SpaceX among its largest positions, trading daily on the NYSE. DXYZ carries a reported expense ratio of approximately 6.28% and has at times traded at substantial premiums to NAV — ranging from significant to extreme — though premium levels have fluctuated considerably.Fundrise Innovation Fund (VCX)The Fundrise Innovation Fund (VCX) lists on the NYSE and holds SpaceX alongside AI, fintech, and aerospace companies. VCX charges 1.85% annually and has at times traded at substantial premiums to NAV, with premium levels varying considerably. Shares acquired before February 20, 2026 may be subject to a six-month lock-up.Interval Funds Offer NAV Pricing But Limited Exit Windows Interval funds are retail-accessible and require no accreditation. Unlike closed-end funds, they price at NAV — eliminating the premium risk described above. The trade-off is liquidity: interval funds offer periodic — typically quarterly — redemption windows that may be subject to a cap, commonly in the range of 5% of outstanding shares per quarter, though terms vary by fund and redemption requests above any cap may be prorated. Investors cannot act on a specific trading day in response to market conditions. For the IPO cycle described earlier, this is a material constraint: redemption windows may not align with the window when an investor would wish to reduce or exit exposure, and results will depend on the specific fund's terms and redemption demand at the time.ARK Venture Fund (ARKVX)The ARK Venture Fund (ARKVX) holds SpaceX alongside a portfolio of private technology and AI companies, with quarterly redemption windows, a $500 minimum, and approximately 2.90% in annual expenses. No accreditation is required, but redemptions may be subject to a quarterly cap.The Private Shares Fund (PRIVX / PIIVX / PRLVX)The Private Shares Fund (PRIVX/PIIVX) has held SpaceX as a significant position and is accessible through Fidelity, Pershing, and Schwab. Expense ratios range from approximately 2.40% to 2.65% depending on share class, with minimums from $2,500 to $1,000,000. Quarterly repurchases may be subject to a cap, and redemption results will depend on fund terms and demand at the time.Secondary Market Platforms Offer Direct Exposure With The Longest Lock-UpsSecondary market platforms — including Forge Global, Hiive, Zanbato, and Nasdaq Private Market (Tape D) — are restricted to accredited investors only and are not available to the general retail public.For those who do qualify, secondary platforms offer the most direct form of SpaceX exposure: investors acquire SpaceX shares or interests in SPVs directly from existing shareholders, including employees and early institutional investors. The critical limitation — particularly relevant to the IPO cycle analysis in this article — is the post-IPO lock-up period.Lock-Up Risk: The Central Issue for Accredited InvestorsTransactions on these platforms are typically subject to post-IPO lock-up periods, often extending six to twelve months, during which investors cannot sell. Transaction fees generally range from 2% to 6% depending on the platform and structure.Platform-Specific ProfilesForge Global is a leading institutional secondary platform with transaction fees of approximately 2% to 4% and minimum transactions typically of $100,000 or more.Hiive is a direct buyer-seller marketplace with a $25,000 minimum and transaction fees of approximately 2% to 3%.Zanbato is oriented toward institutional investors, family offices, and endowments; generally not accessible to retail accredited investors.Nasdaq Private Market (Tape D) provides regulated secondary market infrastructure; post-IPO lock-up restrictions typically apply.What The Lock-Up Variable Means For InvestorsThe IPO data in Section I provides relevant historical context. On average across 13 completed observations, the strongest pricing window — approximately 132% above the IPO price — has historically closed before most locked-up investors were permitted to act, with an average drawdown of 44% from peak to lock-up expiry. This pattern has a logical basis: when lock-ups expire, supply enters the market and prices adjust. Whether that pattern holds for SpaceX is an open question. The S&P 500 inclusion dynamic adds a further layer of complexity: index eligibility may require a larger tradeable float that only becomes available as the lock-up expires, meaning index demand and lock-up supply could arrive simultaneously — with uncertain net effect on price.That structural lens organizes the comparison in this article — though it is equally important to acknowledge that for SpaceX specifically, when any peak pricing window will occur is not a settled question. Index inclusion demand, if it materializes, may arrive at or after lock-up expiry rather than before it, as the float needed for index eligibility may only emerge as locked-up shares are released. The interaction of these forces makes directional prediction difficult. Investors in all structures should weigh the full range of possibilities.For retail investors, the structural picture is clearest at the extremes. ETFs and open-end mutual funds impose no lock-up and provide daily liquidity — the investor retains full optionality throughout the IPO cycle, whenever the most significant pricing moments occur. Secondary market platforms impose a mandatory six-to-twelve-month lock-up and are restricted to accredited investors — the investor is structurally prevented from acting during the lock-up period, whenever that period falls relative to the pricing cycle. Everything else falls between those poles: closed-end funds offer daily trading but embed NAV premium risk as a separate variable; interval funds offer NAV-based pricing but constrain exit timing to quarterly windows.Structure Shapes OutcomesMany investors believe they are gaining access to private markets. In reality, many are gaining access without control — entering structures that lock them in during peak pricing, expose them to premium compression, or limit their ability to respond to changing conditions. The difference is subtle at entry. It is significant at exit.Each structure in this comparison offers genuine trade-offs. No single vehicle eliminates all risks. The lock-up question is worth examining early — alongside fees, concentration, liquidity terms, and an investor’s own time horizon.ConclusionSpaceX may represent the most anticipated liquidity event in a generation of private market investing. With valuations approaching $1.75 trillion and a public listing increasingly expected, the question of how to invest has become as important as whether to invest.The vehicles available to investors differ materially across cost, liquidity, premium risk, and the specific constraint of post-IPO lock-up periods. An investor evaluating these options solely on the basis of the vehicle's name or headline SpaceX exposure risks optimizing for the wrong variable. Each structure in this comparison presents genuine trade-offs, and no single vehicle is appropriate for all investors or all investment objectives.Secondary market platforms provide the most direct SpaceX exposure but impose post-IPO lock-up periods — typically six to twelve months — during which investors cannot act. Historical IPO data shows this is precisely the period when prices have, on average, declined 44% from their peak. However, SpaceX presents dynamics that may not follow that template. The Meta example illustrates that a transformational company can continue appreciating for years beyond the lock-up window. The S&P 500 inclusion dynamic could generate hundreds of billions in structural demand — but that demand may not materialize until the float expands, which could coincide with lock-up expiry rather than precede it; the net effect of simultaneous supply and demand at that moment is not predictable. Closed-end funds provide daily trading liquidity but introduce NAV premium risk as a separate variable. Interval funds offer NAV-based pricing but constrain exit timing to quarterly windows. ETFs and open-end mutual funds provide daily liquidity with no lock-up constraints — preserving optionality regardless of when the most significant pricing events occur.Access determines participation. Structure determines outcome.SpaceX may be a generational opportunity — and the structure through which an investor holds it may matter as much as the investment itself. Whether the most significant pricing window arrives before or after lock-up expiry, whether index inclusion accelerates post-IPO demand, and how long any lock-up will last are all genuinely open questions. The right structure is the one that matches the investor’s actual objectives, constraints, and time horizon.For investors searching how to invest in SpaceX, how to buy SpaceX stock, or how to gain exposure before an IPO: the first step is to understand that direct public ownership is not yet available, and the second is to evaluate which of the available structures most closely matches specific investment objectives. Reports suggest the IPO discussion is real and active, but timing and structure remain subject to change.
